title: Flattening and combining: flatMap, zip and combine
goal: By the end you can draw the timelines of flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge and flatMapLatest, put the slow call where flatMapMerge runs it side by side, and choose between zip, combine and merge for two flows with their own clocks, including what combine drops for a slow collector.
opening:
A table orders ten dishes on one ticket. Each dish has a small recipe card of its own. At the pass, the counter where orders come in, the head cook reads the ticket one line at a time and hands each dish to a helper at a free burner. The stove has four burners, so four dishes cook at once, and ten dishes take three rounds.

Kotlin has an operator for exactly this kitchen, `flatMapMerge`, and the first version people write looks right and cooks one dish at a time. It takes more than three times as long. The trap is a single line: the head cook cooks each dish herself before she hands it over, while four helpers stand at four warm burners with empty pans.

In Buffering, each value travelled on its own across one shelf. Here each value opens a whole flow of its own. In this lesson, we'll find the line that makes the burners take turns, draw the three ways to run those flows, join two flows with `zip` and `combine`, and watch a slow screen make `combine` skip. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `dishes.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { d -> val plate = stove.cook(d); flowOf(plate) }` runs over 10 dishes. Each `cook` call suspends for 100 ms. How long does the order take?
options: 100 ms: all ten at once
300 ms: three rounds of 4, 4 and 2
1,000 ms: one dish at a time
It doesn't compile: the lambda must not suspend
warmup.why: `flatMapMerge` calls the lambda in the one coroutine that reads the outer flow, one dish at a time, before a burner is taken. Cooking inside the lambda therefore adds up. Only the returned flows run side by side, so `flow { emit(stove.cook(d)) }` would give the 300 ms you expected.

sections.h: The flatMapMerge lambda runs one dish at a time, before a burner is free

aside.title: Do I need a flatMap operator at all?
aside.body: Often you don't. If each dish gives exactly one plate and the dishes may cook one after another, `dishes.map { stove.cook(it) }` does the job, and it's easier to read. The KDoc of `flatMapMerge` and `flatMapConcat` says the same: they are discouraged in ordinary application flows, because a suspend call in `map` is enough and straight-line code is easier to reason about. Reach for `flatMapMerge` when you need several at once with a cap, and for the other two when each value really opens a stream of its own.

sections.h: One at a time, side by side, or only the newest: flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge and flatMapLatest
sections.body:
Now give each order a sub-recipe that takes a while. A table keeps changing its mind and sends three orders, 100 ms apart. Each order opens an inner flow in two parts: part a is ready after 50 ms and part b 150 ms later. The run uses **virtual time**, the fake clock of `runTest` that skips over waits, so the numbers come out the same on every run. With `flatMapConcat`, at what time does order 2 come in?

```kotlin
orders().flatMapConcat { n -> dish(n) }     // also try flatMapMerge and flatMapLatest
```

```java
// Closest Java equivalent: concatMap (and flatMap, switchMap) on the same Flux timeline
orders().concatMap(n -> dish(n));
```

Most people say 100. It is 300, and the whole run takes 800 ms. `flatMapConcat` is `map(transform).flattenConcat()`, and `flattenConcat` is one line: `collect { value -> emitAll(value) }`. There is no second coroutine and no channel. The inner flow runs inside the outer's `emit`, which lesson 1 of this track showed is the cook carrying a plate over and standing there while the diner eats. So the waiter who brings the orders stands at the pass until both parts of the dish are done, and his `delay(100)` before the next order starts only after that.

Put `buffer()` in front, and the waiter runs in his own coroutine and leaves orders on a shelf, the shelf from Buffering. The run drops to 600 ms. Reactor's `concatMap` on the same timeline also finishes at 600 ms. It asks for one order at a time too, but the timers in its source kept running while nobody was asking. A `flow { }` body can't do that, because it is suspended in `emit`.

`flatMapMerge` gives each order its own burner. The orders come in at 0, 100 and 200, the parts arrive in completion order (part 1b at 200 comes after part 2a at 150), and the run ends at 400.

`flatMapLatest` throws the old dish away. It is `transformLatest { emitAll(transform(it)) }`, from the same family as `collectLatest` in Buffering. Each new order cancels the inner flow in flight with `ChildCancelledException` ("Child of the scoped flow was cancelled"), waits for it to finish, and starts the next one. So parts 1b and 2b never arrive, and the run ends at 400. The table changed its mind twice, and the kitchen binned two half-made dishes without a word. Reactor's `switchMap` gives the same timeline. This is the shape for a search box that searches as you type, where a new letter makes the old search worthless. Keep the cancelled flow's cleanup short, because the next one waits for it.

The figure draws all three from the Try it's output.

The kitchen picture holds up well here, and it breaks in one useful place. A real waiter can walk back to the table while a dish cooks. In `flatMapConcat` he can't, because the inner flow runs inside his `emit`, so even his own walking waits.

Check yourself: the outer is `for (n in 1..3) { emit(n); delay(100) }`, and each inner is one value after 200 ms. How long does `flatMapConcat` take? All three operators start from one outer flow. Often there are two flows, each with its own clock.

sections.h: Pairs by number with zip, the latest of each with combine
sections.body:
The oven door has a small screen that shows how far the oven still has to climb. Two flows feed it. The thermometer sends a reading every 100 ms, starting at 100 ms: 150, 152, 154 and so on up to 160 °C. The dial sends a value only when someone turns it: 180 at 250 ms, and 200 at 550 ms. A helper joins them with `zip`:

```kotlin
readings.zip(dial) { c, d -> "$c of $d" }          // a zipper
combine(readings, dial) { c, d -> "$c of $d" }     // a slate with the latest of each
merge(tableOrders, takeawayOrders)                 // two queues into one door
```

```java
// Closest Java equivalent: the same three Reactor operators
Flux.zip(readings, dial, (c, d) -> c + " of " + d);
Flux.combineLatest(readings, dial, (c, d) -> c + " of " + d);
Flux.merge(tableOrders, takeawayOrders);
```

`zip` shows two lines: "150 of 180" at 250 ms and "152 of 200" at 550 ms. Then it ends. **zip** pairs the first value of one flow with the first of the other, the second with the second, and stops at the end of the shorter flow, like the teeth of a zipper. The readings' `onCompletion`, a hook that runs once when a flow ends (the next lesson takes it apart), reports `AbortFlowException: Flow was aborted, no more elements needed`, the signed "no more, thanks" note from lesson 2 of this track.

Something else happened too: reading 152 came at 350 ms, not 200. `zip` collects its receiver, `readings`, in the caller's coroutine with no shelf at all. Only the other flow gets a producer coroutine, with a **rendezvous** channel between them, a hand-over where both hands must meet. So each reading's `emit` waits until there is a dial value to pair it with, and the slower side sets the pace. Reactor's `zip` produced the same two pairs, but its thermometer kept ticking every 100 ms, because Reactor asks its sources for values ahead of time. And Flow has only this two-flow `zip`.

Pairing the second reading with the second turn of the dial is the wrong question. The screen needs each reading against the latest dial setting. That is **combine**. Picture a slate with one line per flow. `combine` starts one coroutine per source, and each one writes its newest value on its own line. Nothing comes out until every line has a value. After that, every update produces one output.

So the first line is "152 of 180" at 250 ms: reading 150 had already been wiped off the slate by 152 before the dial had a value. Then come 154, 156 and 158 of 180, then "158 of 200" the moment the dial moves at 550, then "160 of 200" at 600. A source that never emits means no output at all, and `combine` completes when all its sources have completed.

**merge** is the third way to join flows: values come out as they arrive, from either source, like two queues sharing one door. Table orders every 100 ms and takeaway orders every 70 ms come out as takeaway-0 at 70, table-0 at 100, takeaway-1 at 140, and so on. The merged flow ends when the last source ends, and one source that fails cancels the others.

**Pair by number with zip only when the n-th of one belongs with the n-th of the other. For "the latest of each", use combine.**

Check yourself: what does `combine` show if the dial sends 180 at 0 ms, before the first reading? So far the screen drew each line at once. A slow screen changes what `combine` hands it.

sections.h: A slow screen makes combine skip values and slow the thermometer
sections.body:
Put a slow screen behind `combine`. The thermometer ticks every 10 ms, ten times, and is combined with one dial value, 180. The screen needs 100 ms to draw each update. What does it show?

```kotlin
combine(ticks, flowOf(180)) { i, d -> "$i/$d" }
    .collect { screen.draw(it); delay(100) }        // the screen is slow
```

```java
// Closest Java equivalent: combineLatest in front of a subscriber that takes one at a time
Flux.combineLatest(ticks, Flux.just(180), (i, d) -> i + "/" + d)
    .concatMap(v -> screen.draw(v).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), 1);
```

Flow shows 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 10, at 10, 110, 210, 310, 410 and 510 ms. Reactor's `combineLatest` shows all ten, about 100 ms apart, the last at about 1,050 ms on a busy machine. And there is a second effect in Flow: the thermometer itself slowed down. It needed 330 ms to send its ten readings, not 100. The thermometer has never been slow in its life, and now it waits.

The mechanism is a small tray in front of the slate. Each source coroutine puts its update into a channel whose capacity equals the number of flows, here 2, and then calls `yield()`, a suspension point that lets other coroutines run. The loop that fills the slate takes updates in batches. It reads until it sees a second update from a source it already updated in this batch, rewriting that source's line each time, and then calls your lambda once for the batch.

While the screen is busy, updates pile up, and 2 is rewritten by 3 before anyone copies the slate. Once the tray is full, the thermometer's next `send` suspends: in the log, reading 4 is sent at 40 ms and reading 5 not until 120. So `combine` skips values and slows its sources, both at once. Reactor's screen keeps every state of the slate in a queue and draws them all.

It isn't plain **conflation** (keeping only the newest waiting value) either. Pure latest-only would show 1 and then 10. If you care, say which one you want:

| After `combine(...)` | The screen shows |
|---|---|
| nothing | 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, and the thermometer slows |
| `.conflate()` | 1 at 10 ms, then 10 at 110 ms |
| `.buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED)` | all ten, the last at 1,010 ms |

For a screen, skipping is fine: nobody misses a temperature that was already old. For a cooking log, where every reading must be written next to its dial setting, every combination counts, and an unlimited buffer is a memory bill you size yourself.

One more thing not to rely on. Two flows with no waits at all, `combine(flowOf("a0", "a1", "a2"), flowOf("b0", "b1", "b2"))`, give `a0b0, a1b1, a2b2` in Flow and `a2b0, a2b1, a2b2` in Reactor. With sources that never suspend, which pairs you get depends on scheduling.

Check yourself: with the screen at 100 ms per update, would `buffer(10)` instead of `UNLIMITED` keep all ten? Every operator in this lesson also shares one weakness: a single failing source or inner flow cancels all the others, and the whole flow ends.

compare.title: Flattening and combining in Kotlin Flow and in Reactor

java.title: Reactor

kotlin.title: Kotlin Flow

compare.note: The operators line up one for one, and the virtual-time demos give the same timelines for `flatMap` and `flatMapMerge`, and for `switchMap` and `flatMapLatest`. The differences come from how each library moves values. In Flow, a value moves by a suspend call, so whatever is upstream of an `emit` waits for it: `flatMapConcat` pauses the outer's code (800 ms against Reactor's 600 on the same timeline), and `zip` slows its receiver to the other side's pace. Reactor moves values on demand and asks ahead of time, so its sources keep their own timers. The defaults differ too: 16 lanes against 256. And with a slow subscriber, `combineLatest` queues every state of the slate while `combine` skips some and makes its sources wait. Flow has no built-in `flatMapSequential`.

worked.title: Cook a ticket on four burners

steps.say: The stove has four burners. Put the cooking inside the returned flow, so each dish gets a lane, and set the cap from the stove. Ten dishes of 100 ms are ready at 300 ms.

The salad burns. Catch it inside that dish's own inner flow, so only that lane ends with a substitute. With soup at 300 ms, salad at 100 (burnt) and roast at 200, the plates are the salad's substitute at 100, roast at 200 and soup at 300.

Compare a `catch` placed after `flatMapMerge`. The burnt lane cancels its siblings first: soup and roast end with a `JobCancellationException`, and the `catch` sees `Burnt: burnt: salad` at 100 ms. A caught error still ends the upstream, so this `catch` can only send out a stand-in after every other dish was thrown away.
steps.code:
dishes.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { dish -> flow { emit(stove.cook(dish)) } }
    .catch { emit(Plate("bread basket", "substitute")) }   // too late: the other dishes are already off the stove

steps.say: The cooking log wants the plates in ticket order. Flow has no `flatMapSequential`. Start each dish with `async`, keep up to n of them in flight with a buffer, and wait for them in order. The `buffer(n - 2)` counts the buffer's slots plus one dish being awaited and one being started, so n must be at least 2. Twenty dishes of 100 ms take 1,000, 700, 500 and 300 ms for n = 2, 3, 4 and 8, always in ticket order.

drill.title: Write a capped fan-out from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `fun <T, R> Flow<T>.mergeLanes(lanes: Int, transform: suspend (T) -> Flow<R>): Flow<R>` with `channelFlow`, a `Semaphore` and `launch`. Then answer: in your version, which line runs one value at a time, and why must the slow call not be in `transform`?

recap: `flatMapMerge` calls your lambda one value at a time, in the one coroutine that reads the outer flow, before it takes a lane. Only the returned flows run side by side, so the slow call belongs inside them.
The cap defaults to 16 (`DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY`), against Reactor's 256. Set it from what the slow resource can take. Results come out in completion order.

`flatMapConcat` runs each inner inside the outer's `emit`, so the outer's own code pauses. `buffer()` in front lets it run ahead, which gives Reactor's `concatMap` timeline. `flatMapLatest` cancels the old inner, waits for it and starts the new one.

`zip` pairs by number, slows its receiver to the other side's pace and ends with the shorter flow. `combine` keeps the latest of each and emits once every source has a value. A reading against the latest dial setting is `combine`.
With a slow collector, `combine` skips some values and suspends its sources. Add `conflate()` or `buffer()` to choose; Reactor's `combineLatest` keeps them all.
The limit: one failing inner flow or source cancels all the others and ends the whole flow. Choosing what a failure costs is the next lesson's job.
closing:
We started with a ticket of ten dishes and a head cook who cooked each one before handing it over. `flatMapMerge` runs only the returned flows side by side, `flatMapConcat` holds the outer inside `emit`, and `flatMapLatest` bins the old dish. `zip` pairs by number, `combine` keeps the latest of each, and a slow screen makes it skip.

Now look in your own code for a `flatMapMerge` whose lambda calls a suspend function before it returns `flowOf(...)`. That call runs one value at a time.

Next, we'll drop a plate on purpose. When a flow fails halfway, which `catch` hears it, and what does a retry cook again?

quiz.q:
Which call runs with up to 4 at once?

```kotlin
dishes.flatMapMerge(4) { d ->
    val card = cookbook.open(d)                // suspends 50 ms
    flow { emit(stove.cook(d, card)) }         // suspends 100 ms
}
```
options: Both: flatMapMerge makes the whole lambda run side by side
Only `stove.cook`; `cookbook.open` runs one dish at a time
Only `cookbook.open`; the inner flow is collected later, one at a time
Neither, because `flow { }` inside a lambda is cold
quiz.why: The lambda runs in the one coroutine that reads the outer flow, one dish at a time and before a lane is taken. Only the returned flow gets a lane. So the 50 ms `open` calls add up one after another, while the cooking overlaps. Move `open` into the inner flow if it should overlap too.

quiz.q: The outer is `flow { for (n in 1..3) { emit(n); delay(100) } }` and each inner is one value after 200 ms. `flatMapConcat` takes 900 ms. How long with `.buffer()` before `flatMapConcat`?
options: 600 ms
300 ms
800 ms
900 ms: buffer doesn't change a concat
quiz.why: Without the buffer, each inner runs inside the outer's `emit`, so the outer's `delay(100)` waits for it: 3 x (200 + 100). With the buffer, the outer runs ahead in its own coroutine and the three inners run back to back: 3 x 200 = 600 ms.

quiz.q: The oven screen shows each thermometer reading against the latest dial setting. Readings come every second; the dial changes now and then. Which operator fits?
options: `readings.zip(dial)`
`merge(readings, dial)`
`readings.flatMapLatest { dial }`
`combine(readings, dial)`
quiz.why: `combine` keeps the latest value of each flow and emits on every update of either, once both have a value. `zip` would pair the n-th reading with the n-th turn of the dial and hold the thermometer until the dial moves again. `merge` doesn't pair values at all. The `flatMapLatest` version restarts the dial flow on every reading and emits dial values, not readings against the dial.

quiz.q: `combine(ticks, flowOf(180))` feeds a screen that needs 100 ms per update. The ticks are 1 to 10, 10 ms apart. What happens?
options: The screen shows all ten, 100 ms apart
The screen shows only 1 and 10
The screen shows 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, and the ticks themselves slow down
combine fails with an overflow error
quiz.why: `combine`'s tray holds one update per source. While the screen is busy, updates in the same batch overwrite each other, and once the tray is full the ticking source's `send` suspends. So it both skips and slows its source. All ten is Reactor's `combineLatest`, or Flow with `buffer(UNLIMITED)`. Only 1 and 10 is `conflate()`.

quiz.q: From the reactive track: on the same timeline, Reactor's `concatMap` finished at 600 ms and Kotlin's `flatMapConcat` at 800 ms. Why?
options: Reactor's concatMap asks its source for 32 items ahead
Flow's outer code is suspended inside `emit` while each inner runs, so its own delays start late; Reactor's source timers kept running
flatMapConcat runs the inners on Dispatchers.Default
Flow's flatMapConcat runs two inners at once
quiz.why: `flatMapConcat` is `collect { emitAll(it) }`: no coroutine and no channel, so the outer's body waits in `emit`. Reactor 3.8's `concatMap` asks for one at a time too, but its source's `Mono.delay` timers ran while no request was outstanding. `buffer()` before `flatMapConcat` gives Flow the same 600 ms.

flashcards.front: In `flatMapMerge`, does the lambda run side by side for several values?
flashcards.back: No. It runs one value at a time, in the one coroutine that reads the outer flow, before a lane is taken. Only the flows it returns run side by side.

flashcards.front: Default concurrency of `flatMapMerge`, and of Reactor's `flatMap`?
What happens to the outer flow while a `flatMapConcat` inner runs?
flashcards.back: Its code is paused inside `emit`: there is no extra coroutine or channel. `buffer()` before `flatMapConcat` lets it run ahead.

flashcards.front: `flatMapLatest` gets a new value while an inner is running. What happens?
flashcards.back: It cancels the inner with `ChildCancelledException`, waits for it to finish, then starts the inner for the new value.

flashcards.front: How does `zip` pair values, and when does it end?
flashcards.back: By number: first with first, second with second. It ends when the shorter flow ends and cancels the other. Its receiver has no buffer, so it waits for the other side.

flashcards.front: When does `combine` emit its first value?
flashcards.back: When every source has emitted at least once. After that, once per update of any source.

flashcards.front: `combine` with a slow collector: what happens to fast updates?
flashcards.back: Some are skipped (overwritten on the slate) and the sources are suspended, since the tray holds one update per source. Reactor's `combineLatest` delivers them all.

terms.plain: Turning a flow of flows (one inner flow per outer value) into one flow of values.
The flow your `flatMap*` lambda returns for one outer value: a dish's own sub-recipe.
One inner flow being collected in its own coroutine. `concurrency` is the number of lanes, the burners on the stove.
Results leave in the order they are ready, not the order their inputs arrived.
Pairs the n-th value of one flow with the n-th value of another, and ends with the shorter.
Keeps the latest value of each flow and emits a combination whenever any of them changes.
Passes on values from several flows in the order they arrive, and ends when the last one ends.

explain_back.prompt: A helper's order uses `flatMapMerge(concurrency = 8)`, yet the kitchen log shows one dish on the stove at a time. Explain why, how you'd fix it, and how you'd keep one burnt dish from ruining the rest. Use the head cook at the pass.
explain_back.answer: `flatMapMerge` has one head cook at the pass: a single coroutine reads the dishes and calls the lambda for each one, one at a time, before it hands the result to a burner. The burners are the 8 lanes, and only the flow the lambda returns is collected on a burner. The helper cooks the dish in the lambda itself and returns `flowOf(plate)`, so the head cook cooks every dish herself and the burners stay empty: one dish at a time. The fix is to return `flow { emit(stove.cook(dish)) }`, so the cooking runs in the lane. To keep one burnt dish from taking the others down, put `catch` on that dish's inner flow and emit a substitute there. A `catch` after `flatMapMerge` comes too late, because the burnt lane has already cancelled all the other lanes.

deeper.body:
How far does `flatMapMerge` run ahead of a slow collector? With 500 one-value inners and a collector stuck on its first value, 82 outer values had been pulled. A likely split (my inference, not measured) is 64 results in the output channel, about 16 inners suspended on a full channel, and a couple in hand. With `.buffer(0)` after it the count was 18, and with `flatMapConcat` it was 1. So budget memory for up to 64 finished results plus `concurrency` inners. A `buffer` or `flowOn` after `flatMapMerge` fuses into the same channel: `flatMapMerge(4) { }.buffer(0)` prints as `ChannelFlowMerge[concurrency=4, capacity=0]`.

Edge cases: `flatMapMerge(1)` returns plain `flattenConcat()`. `flatMapMerge(0)` throws `IllegalArgumentException: Expected positive concurrency level, but had 0` when you build the flow. Setting `-Dkotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency=0` makes the first read of `DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY` throw `ExceptionInInitializerError`, caused by `IllegalStateException: System property 'kotlinx.coroutines.flow.defaultConcurrency' should be in range 1..2147483647, but is '0'`. With `=4`, 40 dishes of 100 ms took 1,000 ms instead of 300.

`flattenConcat()` and `flattenMerge()` are the same operators for a `Flow<Flow<T>>` you already have; `flatMapX(f)` is literally `map(f).flattenX()`.

`combineTransform` is `combine` with a `FlowCollector` receiver, so the lambda can emit zero or several values per update of the slate. Failure works the same way in `combine` and `merge`: one source that throws cancels the others (they end with `JobCancellationException: Parent job is Cancelling`) and the caller gets the original exception.
